howItWorks.intro: This calculator works backward from the income you want to take home to the billable rate that actually produces it, closing the gap between a salary figure and a freelance calendar's realities.

rules.name: Annual Billable Hours
rules.formula: Billable Hours = Billable Hours per Week × (52 − Weeks Off)
rules.explanation: Only hours you can actually invoice count. Admin, marketing, proposal writing, and unpaid time off are excluded before the rate is ever set — they don't disappear, they just don't get billed.

rules.name: Rate Needed Per Billable Hour
rules.formula: Hourly Rate = [Target Income ÷ (1 − Overhead %)] ÷ Annual Billable Hours
rules.explanation: Target income is grossed up to cover business overhead and the self-employment tax bite, then spread across the smaller pool of billable hours instead of total hours worked.

howItWorks.outro: Treat the result as a floor, not a ceiling. A rate that only covers income, tax, and overhead leaves nothing for raises, slow months, or the retirement contributions a salaried job would otherwise fund on your behalf.

faq.question: Why is the rate here so much higher than my target salary divided by 2,080 hours?
faq.answer: Because 2,080 hours assumes every hour you work gets billed, and that none of your income is lost to self-employment tax. In practice, admin, marketing, and unpaid time off typically remove 20–35% of your working hours from the billable pool, and self-employment tax takes roughly 15.3% of net earnings before overhead is even factored in. Both gaps push the real rate well above a simple salary ÷ hours figure.

faq.question: What exactly counts as non-billable time?
faq.answer: Proposal writing, client communication that isn't on a paid clock, invoicing and bookkeeping, marketing and networking, professional development, and any unpaid sick days, holidays, or vacation. For most independent contractors this runs 15–30% of total working hours, even in a busy year — it's time spent running the business, not doing the billable work.

faq.question: Is 15.3% the right self-employment tax figure to use?
faq.answer: 15.3% covers the combined Social Security and Medicare portion of self-employment tax on net earnings — the cost a traditional employer would otherwise split with you. It doesn't include federal or state income tax, so your real tax-driven markup may need to run higher depending on your bracket, deductions, and state.

faq.question: Should health insurance count as business overhead?
faq.answer: Either treatment works as long as you're consistent. If you buy your own coverage, folding the premium into your overhead percentage means it gets funded by your rate directly, instead of quietly eating into the take-home income you were trying to hit.

faq.question: What if I only freelance part-time alongside a regular job?
faq.answer: Use a lower weekly billable-hours figure and set your target income to whatever amount you want the freelance work alone to produce. The same gross-up for self-employment tax and overhead still applies — those costs don't shrink just because the work is part-time.

howWeCalculate.intro: The math runs in two passes: first narrowing your total work year down to the hours you can actually invoice, then grossing up your income target to cover costs a paycheck normally absorbs for you.
steps: Start with your target annual income — the take-home amount you're trying to replace or exceed as a freelancer.

Subtract non-billable time from your work year: client admin, marketing and outreach, proposal writing, professional development, and any unpaid sick days or vacation, to find your realistic annual billable hours.
Gross up the target income to account for self-employment tax (≈15.3% of net earnings) and recurring business overhead such as software, insurance, and equipment.
Divide the grossed-up income by your annual billable hours to get the rate each billable hour actually needs to carry.
howWeCalculate.disclaimer: This figure estimates the rate needed to hit an income target given your inputs. Actual tax liability depends on deductions, filing status, and state rules, so confirm numbers with an accountant before setting contracts.

whenToUse.intro: This conversion matters most at the moments when you're translating a dollar goal into a number a client will actually see on an invoice.
scenarios: Leaving a salaried job and trying to figure out what hourly rate replaces your old paycheck, benefits included.
Your billable utilization has dropped — more time going to proposals, admin, or marketing than last year — and your old rate no longer covers your income target.
You're about to take unpaid time off (parental leave, a sabbatical, extended travel) and need to see how fewer billable hours changes the rate on remaining work.
You're budgeting for new overhead — liability insurance, a coworking membership, new equipment — and want to know how much of that cost has to flow into your rate.
You're comparing a retainer or flat-project offer against your hourly floor to make sure it isn't quietly underpaying you.

sections.title: Why Dividing Salary by 2,000 Hours Shortchanges You
sections.body: Most freelancers price their time by picking a target income and dividing by 2,000 — the classic 40 hours × 50 weeks. That shortcut assumes every one of those 2,000 hours gets billed to a client. It never does. Between writing proposals, chasing invoices, posting on LinkedIn, learning new tools, and the week you take off sick without pay, a sizeable chunk of the work year produces zero revenue. A rate built on 2,000 hours is a rate built on a number that doesn't exist in your actual calendar.

sections.title: Three Gaps a Paycheck Already Closes for You
sections.body: Converting a target income into a billable hourly rate means closing three gaps a traditional paycheck handles quietly in the background. First, non-billable time — admin, marketing, proposals, unpaid sick days and vacation — routinely eats 15–30% of a freelancer's working hours, so the hours you can actually invoice sit well below your total hours worked. Second, self-employment tax: as a sole proprietor you cover both the employee and employer share of Social Security and Medicare, roughly 15.3% of net self-employment earnings, a cost a W-2 employer absorbs on your behalf. Third, overhead — software subscriptions, business insurance, a portion of your home office, accounting fees, equipment — expenses a salaried job simply never bills you for. Each gap has to be folded into the rate before you multiply by a single hour.

sections.title: Worked Example: Turning $90,000 Into a Real Hourly Rate
sections.body: Say you want your freelance income to feel like a $90,000 salary. A freelancer working 40-hour weeks for 50 weeks a year has 2,000 nominal work hours — but after subtracting time spent on admin, marketing, and unpaid time off (commonly 20% of the work year), only about 1,600 of those hours are actually billable. Divide $90,000 by 2,000 and you get $45/hour — a number that looks reasonable and is quietly wrong. Instead, gross up $90,000 to cover self-employment tax (≈15.3%) and business overhead (say 10%): $90,000 ÷ (1 − 0.153 − 0.10) = $90,000 ÷ 0.747 ≈ $120,482. That's the revenue your business actually needs to collect in a year. Divide that by the 1,600 hours you can realistically bill, and the rate comes out to roughly $75.30/hour — about 67% higher than the naive $45 figure, and the number that actually funds a $90,000 lifestyle once taxes and overhead are paid.

howToSteps.title: Enter the income you're targeting
howToSteps.description: Input the annual income figure you want your freelance work to produce — the number you're replacing or aiming for, before tax and overhead are layered on top.

howToSteps.title: Set your realistic billable hours per week
howToSteps.description: Enter the hours you expect to actually invoice in a typical week, not your total working hours. If a third of your week goes to admin and outreach, your billable hours sit lower than your desk time.

howToSteps.title: Account for weeks you won't bill
howToSteps.description: Enter the weeks per year you expect to take off, paid or not — vacation, illness, slow seasons. Every week off shrinks the pool of hours left to carry your income target.

howToSteps.title: Add your business overhead percentage
howToSteps.description: Include software, insurance, equipment, and other recurring costs as a share of revenue, then run the calculation to see the hourly rate that actually funds your target income after tax and overhead.

tips: Track your actual billable hours for a month before trusting a 'standard' utilization rate — many freelancers bill closer to 50–70% of hours worked, not the 80% often assumed.
Set aside for self-employment tax as it's earned, not at filing time — 15.3% of net profit on top of income tax adds up fast if it isn't priced into your rate from day one.
Recalculate when your overhead changes — adding health insurance, a new software subscription, or a coworking desk should flow straight into your rate, not get absorbed silently.
Price unpaid time off into your rate, not into guilt — if you want two weeks away each year, that time has to be funded by the weeks you do bill.
Revisit the rate annually rather than waiting for a client to push back — mid-negotiation is the wrong moment to discover your rate was undercosted from the start.
